posts.title: How Often Should You Repaint Your Commercial Building's Exterior?
posts.excerpt: Paint doesn't fail on a fixed schedule. Here's how to actually tell when your building's exterior needs attention — and what happens if you wait too long.
posts.author: Bauer Painting Team
content: "Every 5 to 7 years" is the answer most people expect, and it's a reasonable starting point — but the real answer depends on your building's material, exposure, and the quality of the original paint job far more than the calendar does.
## What actually wears paint out

Sun exposure, freeze-thaw cycles, and moisture are the three biggest factors. A south-facing wall in direct sun will fade and chalk years before a shaded north wall on the same building. Stucco and masonry hold paint longer than wood or metal siding, but they show different failure signs when they do go.
## Signs it's time, regardless of age
- Chalking — a powdery residue that rubs off on your hand when you touch the wall
- Visible fading or colour shift, especially compared to a protected area like under an awning
- Cracking, peeling, or bubbling paint, even in small patches
- Rust streaks near metal fixtures, flashing, or fasteners
- Caulking that's cracked or pulled away from joints and trim

Any one of these on its own isn't an emergency. Several at once, especially cracking or peeling, means moisture is already getting behind the paint film — and that's when small maintenance jobs turn into larger repair jobs.
## Why waiting costs more than painting early

Paint isn't just cosmetic on a commercial building — it's the first line of defense against water intrusion. Once a paint film fails, the substrate underneath is exposed, and repairs (rot, spalling masonry, rusted steel) cost far more than a repaint would have. A proactive maintenance cycle is almost always cheaper over a 10-year window than a reactive one.
If you're not sure where your building stands, a walk-through assessment is a fast way to find out — we offer these as part of every quote.

posts.title: 5 Signs It's Time to Repaint Your Office Interior
posts.excerpt: Your office walls take a quiet beating every day. Here are the signs that tell you it's time for a refresh, before they start affecting how your space feels.
posts.author: Bauer Painting Team
content: Interior wear is easy to miss because it happens gradually, in a space you walk through every day. Here's what to look for.
## 1. Scuffs and marks that don't wipe clean
High-traffic areas like hallways, near desks, and around doorways accumulate scuffs faster than most people notice — until a client or new hire points it out.
## 2. Dated or mismatched colours
A rebrand, an office expansion, or simply a decade of touch-ups in slightly different shades can leave a space feeling disjointed rather than intentional.
## 3. Yellowing near light fixtures and vents
Older paint, especially in break rooms and near HVAC returns, can yellow or discolour over time — a sign the finish has aged past its useful life.
## 4. Visible patchwork from past repairs
- Touch-up spots that don't quite match the surrounding wall
- Drywall repairs that were never fully blended in
- Different sheens visible under office lighting
## 5. It just doesn't feel like a place people want to be in
This one's harder to quantify, but it matters. Interior finish quality has a real effect on how staff and clients perceive a space — and by extension, your business.
A fresh coat is one of the highest-impact, lowest-disruption upgrades you can make to a commercial interior. Most projects can be scheduled around business hours or overnight with no downtime at all.

posts.title: Choosing the Right Paint Finish for High-Traffic Commercial Areas
posts.excerpt: Colour gets all the attention, but finish is what determines how well your paint job actually holds up in a busy commercial space.
posts.author: Bauer Painting Team
content: Sheen level affects durability, cleanability, and how forgiving a wall is of everyday wear — and picking the wrong one is one of the most common (and avoidable) mistakes in commercial painting.
## The sheen spectrum, from lowest to highest
- Flat/matte — best hides surface imperfections, but marks easily and is hard to clean. Best for low-traffic ceilings and formal spaces.
- Eggshell — a good middle ground for offices and meeting rooms; some washability without much shine.
- Satin — the workhorse finish for hallways, common areas, and most commercial interiors. Wipes clean, holds up well.
- Semi-gloss — ideal for trim, doors, kitchens, and washrooms where moisture and cleaning are frequent.
- High-gloss — maximum durability and shine, typically reserved for handrails, doors, and accent details.
## Matching finish to the room

Restaurants and healthcare facilities generally lean toward satin or semi-gloss throughout, since cleanability matters more than in a typical office. Warehouses and industrial spaces often use durable epoxy or industrial enamel systems rather than standard commercial paint entirely.
## A quick rule of thumb
The more a surface gets touched, bumped, or cleaned, the higher the sheen should be. Trim, doors, and high-traffic walls generally want a step up in sheen from the surrounding field colour.
If you're not sure what's right for your space, this is exactly the kind of thing we walk through during a project assessment — the right finish choice up front saves a repaint down the line.

posts.title: How We Minimize Disruption When Painting Occupied Buildings
posts.excerpt: Painting a building while it's still in use is a scheduling and logistics problem as much as a painting one. Here's how we approach it.
posts.author: Bauer Painting Team
content: Most of our commercial clients don't have the option to close down while a project is underway — so minimizing disruption isn't an add-on, it's a core part of how we plan every job.
## Scheduling around your operations

We work nights, weekends, or in phases depending on what keeps your business running. For offices, that often means painting after hours. For retail and hospitality, it can mean working section by section during off-peak times rather than closing entirely.
## Containment and protection
- Furniture, equipment, and flooring are covered and protected before any prep work begins
- Dust and odour containment barriers are used in occupied areas
- Low-VOC, low-odour products are used wherever occupants will be nearby during or shortly after painting
## Clear communication throughout

A project only runs smoothly if everyone knows what to expect. We provide a schedule up front, flag any areas that will be inaccessible on a given day, and do a final walkthrough with you before considering the job complete.
The goal on every occupied-building project is the same: a finished space that looks like nothing was ever disrupted at all.

posts.title: Commercial vs. Residential Painting: What's Actually Different
posts.excerpt: It's not just a bigger version of a house paint job. Here's what actually changes when a project is commercial.
posts.author: Bauer Painting Team
content: On the surface, painting is painting — but commercial projects come with a different set of priorities than a typical residential job.
## Scale and scheduling
Commercial projects are often larger, span multiple crews, and have to work around business hours, tenants, or the public rather than a single homeowner's schedule.
## Product selection
- Commercial-grade coatings are formulated for higher durability and heavier cleaning cycles
- Industrial environments often need specialized systems (epoxy, dryfall, anti-corrosive coatings)
- Fire-rating and code compliance can factor into product choice in institutional and public buildings
## Documentation and compliance

Commercial work often involves site safety protocols, insurance and WSIB documentation, and sometimes coordination with a building's own facilities or property management team — requirements a typical residential job simply doesn't have.

None of this makes commercial painting more complicated to work with as a client — it just means the contractor needs the systems and experience to manage it well. That's the part we focus on getting right on every project.
